title: Item memorability has no influence on value-based decisions
authors: Xinyue Li, Wilma A. Bainbridge, Akram Bakkour
caption_short: Continuous recognition memorability task: participants view a stream of single-object photographs (1 s each, separated by a fixation cross) and press the 'r' key when an image repeats after a delay of more than 120 s.
notes: FALLBACK FIGURE - NOT from the original THINGS-memorability paper. The original dataset paper (Kramer, Hebart, Baker & Bainbridge, 'The features underlying the memorability of objects', Science Advances 9:eadd2981, 2023, https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.add2981, CC BY-NC 4.0, saved as site/papers/things_mem.pdf) contains NO task-paradigm figure: its four main figures (Figs. 1-4) and its seven supplementary figures (figs. S1-S7) are all analysis plots, and the bioRxiv preprint (10.1101/2022.04.29.490104, saved as site/papers/things_mem_preprint.pdf, retrieved via the Wayback Machine because biorxiv.org serves a Cloudflare challenge) has the same four figures. The project OSF repository (https://osf.io/5a7z6) contains only data tables, no task diagram. The figure used here is Figure 1A of Li, Bainbridge & Bakkour (2022), a study from the same senior lab (W. A. Bainbridge) that uses the same online continuous-recognition repeat-detection paradigm with single-object photographs and the same 'r' key response; PDF saved as site/papers/things_mem_paradigm_fallback.pdf. Differences from the actual THINGS experiment as described in the Science Advances Methods: THINGS used 500 ms image presentation with an 800 ms interstimulus interval, a minimum 60 s (not 120 s) delay before a target repeat, vigilance repeats 1-5 images apart, and 187 THINGS object images per participant (N = 13,946 AMT participants). Crop is panel A only; panel B (a value-based choice task, irrelevant here) and the caption are excluded. Rendered at 220 dpi.
